claims.text: In AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles, surface-energy minimization rather than sluggish diffusion drives Au and Cu surface segregation.
Au and Cu are lower-surface-energy elements relative to the other components of the alloy.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the bulk FCC structure.
For sub-5 nm particles, surface-energy terms dominate the Gibbs free energy because of the high surface-to-volume ratio.
Segregation of Au and Cu to the nanoparticle surface lowers the total system energy.
Surface-segregated Au and Cu subsequently evaporate.
Au and Cu evaporate because their boiling points are relatively low compared with those of Pt, Ni, and Co.
Selective evaporation leads to particle shrinkage and coalescence.
The mechanism becomes dominant at approximately 600-800 K.
At approximately 600-800 K, the surface-diffusion activation barrier is overcome, enabling rapid segregation and evaporation.
Initial nanoparticle shape affects the surface-energy gradient and therefore the segregation and evaporation rates.
Icosahedral particles have higher-energy facets and segregate and evaporate faster than truncated-octahedral particles.
The proposed surface-driven mechanism is not limited by sluggish bulk diffusion.
The mechanism produces progressive loss of sub-5 nm particles.
The mechanism widens the nanoparticle size distribution.
The mechanism reshapes particles from elliptical to spherical geometries.
During segregation and evaporation, the particle interior remains FCC while its composition changes over time.
The mechanism is dominant for sub-10 nm particles, whereas bulk diffusion may dominate in larger particles.
The critical temperature and relative contributions of surface energy and bulk diffusion depend on synthesis conditions, morphology, and composition.
